title: Use standard section headings
text: Applicant tracking systems map resume sections by their heading. Use conventional names such as Summary, Skills, Work Experience, Projects, Education and Certifications. Creative headings like 'My Journey' or 'Toolbox' can cause the section to be misfiled or ignored.

title: List experience in reverse chronological order
text: Place the most recent role first and include a start and end date for every position. Parsers build your career timeline from these dates, and gaps or missing dates make the timeline unreliable.

title: Order sections by relevance
text: Experienced candidates lead with Summary, Skills and Experience, then Education. Students and freshers can lead with Education and Projects. Put the strongest evidence for the target role in the top third of page one.

title: Prefer a simple single-column layout
text: Multi-column layouts, text boxes, tables, headers and footers and graphics can scramble reading order when parsed. A clean single-column layout keeps text in the order a human reads it.

title: Avoid icons, images and skill-rating graphics
text: Skill bars, star ratings, charts and icons carry no machine-readable text. Write skills as plain text. Photos are often ignored or discouraged by company hiring portals, so omit them unless the region expects one.

title: Use standard, readable fonts
text: Fonts such as Calibri, Arial, Helvetica, Georgia and Times New Roman render and parse reliably. Keep body text between 10 and 12 points and headings clearly distinguishable by size or weight rather than by color alone.

title: Use plain bullet characters
text: Standard round bullets parse cleanly. Decorative symbols, arrows or emoji can turn into unreadable characters in plain-text conversions.

title: Submit a text-based PDF or DOCX
text: Export from a text-based source so the file contains real, selectable text. Scanned images of a resume cannot be read by an ATS. Follow the posting's stated file format if one is given.

title: Put complete contact details at the top
text: Include full name, a professional email, a phone number with country code, city and state, and relevant profile links such as LinkedIn or GitHub. Keep contact details in the page body rather than in a header or footer where parsers may skip them.

title: Use a professional email address
text: Use an address based on your name. Avoid nicknames and outdated providers. The email is often the unique key used to deduplicate and identify candidates.

title: Write profile links in a parseable form
text: Use full URLs or clear link text such as linkedin.com/in/yourname. Make sure GitHub and portfolio links work and point to projects that match the resume.

title: Write a focused 3-4 line summary
text: Open with your target role and years of experience or academic focus, then name your strongest technologies and one concrete outcome. Mirror the job title and a few core keywords. Avoid first-person pronouns and generic claims such as 'hard-working team player'.

title: Start every bullet with a strong action verb
text: Lead with verbs such as Built, Designed, Implemented, Optimized, Reduced, Led or Automated. Avoid weak openers like 'Responsible for', 'Worked on', 'Helped' or 'Assisted', which hide what you actually did.

title: Quantify achievements
text: Add numbers wherever you honestly can: users or requests served, percentage improvement, time or cost saved, team size, data volume or test coverage. Metrics make impact credible and comparable. If you do not know an exact figure, use a defensible estimate or describe scale instead.

title: Structure bullets as action, context and result
text: A strong bullet states what you did, how or with what, and the outcome. For example: built a REST API with Spring Boot and PostgreSQL that cut report generation time by 40 percent. One achievement per bullet.

title: Keep bullets to one or two lines
text: Aim for roughly 10 to 25 words per bullet and 3 to 6 bullets per role, with the most relevant first. Very long bullets are skimmed and very short ones carry little keyword value.

title: Mirror the job posting's keywords naturally
text: Recruiters search ATS databases by keyword. Use the exact terms from the posting, such as 'Spring Boot' or 'CI/CD', and only for skills you truly have. Include both the spelled-out form and the acronym once, for example 'Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD)'.

title: Show keywords in context, not only in a skills list
text: A skill listed only in a skills section proves little. Repeat key technologies inside experience or project bullets so both the ATS and the recruiter see where and how you used them.

title: Do not keyword-stuff
text: Hidden text, repeated keyword blocks or unrelated buzzwords can be detected and rejected, and they damage credibility with human readers. Keywords should appear where they honestly belong.

title: Prioritize required over preferred skills
text: Cover every required skill you genuinely have before nice-to-haves. If a required skill is missing, show the closest related experience and a relevant project rather than claiming it.

title: Group skills into labeled categories
text: Use categories such as Languages, Frameworks, Databases, Cloud and DevOps, and Tools. Grouped skills are easier to scan and parse than one long comma-separated list. Order each group with the most job-relevant skill first.

title: List only skills you can discuss
text: Every listed skill can be tested in an interview. Prefer fewer, genuine skills over an exhaustive list, and indicate depth through experience bullets rather than self-rated bars.

title: Make projects show real engineering
text: For each project give the name, a one-line purpose, the technology stack, a link, and two or three bullets covering what you built, the design choice, and the measurable result. Projects are the strongest evidence for students and career changers.

title: Treat internships like real roles
text: List company, role, location and dates, and use the same action-and-result bullets as for jobs. Describe the tools you used and what shipped or improved.

title: Present education clearly
text: Give the degree, field, institution, dates and CGPA or percentage, particularly within the first few years after graduation. Add relevant coursework or honors only if space allows.

title: Include relevant certifications with issuer and year
text: List the certification name, issuing organization and date, and a credential link if available. Prioritize certifications that match the target role and technologies.

title: Support achievements with context
text: Awards, hackathon results and ranks are stronger with the organizer, the scale and the year, for example 'Winner among 120 teams'. Keep them brief and relevant.

title: Keep the resume to one or two pages
text: One page suits early-career candidates. Two pages suit extensive experience. Trim older or irrelevant roles rather than shrinking fonts. Aim for roughly 300 to 700 words of focused content.

title: Format dates consistently
text: Use one format throughout, such as 'Aug 2024 - Present'. Inconsistent or ambiguous dates confuse timeline parsing and may be read as gaps.

title: Use consistent tense
text: Use present tense for your current role and past tense for earlier roles and completed projects. Consistency reads as professional and polished.

title: Avoid first-person pronouns
text: Resume writing omits 'I', 'me' and 'my'. Start phrases with the action instead, which is shorter and standard.

title: Spell out less common acronyms once
text: Write the full term with the acronym in brackets on first use, such as 'Object-Relational Mapping (ORM)'. This matches both spellings that a recruiter might search.

title: Align your headline with the target job title
text: If you are targeting a specific role, use a matching title near the top, such as 'Java Backend Developer', as long as it is truthful for your experience. Title matches are a common first-pass filter.

title: Tailor the resume for each application
text: Adjust the summary, skill order and top bullets to the specific posting. Keep one master resume and create a targeted version per application.

title: Explain gaps and career changes briefly
text: If there is a gap, add a short factual line such as 'Career break - upskilling in cloud engineering' with relevant projects or courses. Clear context is better than unexplained empty time.

title: Proofread for spelling and consistency
text: Typos in skill names or job titles can make a keyword unsearchable and signal carelessness. Check technology capitalization, for example JavaScript, PostgreSQL and GitHub.

title: Freshers: lead with projects, skills and internships
text: Without full-time experience, demonstrate capability through well-described projects, internships, certifications and hackathons. Use the same quantified, action-led bullets and a clear technology stack for each.

title: Experienced candidates: show scope and leadership
text: Highlight the scale you worked at, systems you owned, people you mentored and measurable business impact. Keep earlier roles concise.

title: Back claims with verifiable links
text: Link to GitHub repositories, live demos or credentials where possible. Verifiable evidence adds trust and gives recruiters a quick way to confirm skills.
